misconceptions.statement: There is no gravity in space, so satellites float because gravity is absent.
misconceptions.why: Astronauts look weightless in videos, so students think gravity is zero up there.
misconceptions.fix: Gravity at satellite height is still strong, nearly as much as on the ground. Satellites and astronauts seem weightless because they are in free fall around Earth.

probe.question: Why does a satellite 400 km above Earth keep going around the Earth?
probe.wrong_answer: Because there is no gravity there, so nothing pulls it down.

misconceptions.root_belief: what looks weightless has no gravity acting
misconceptions.source_hint: science education research on children's ideas about gravity and weightlessness

misconceptions.statement: A satellite stays up because it is so high that it has escaped Earth's pull.
misconceptions.why: Students think things fall only when close to the ground.
misconceptions.fix: A satellite is always falling towards Earth but moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing it. Gravity is what keeps it in orbit.

probe.question: If gravity switched off, what would happen to a satellite?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, it would keep circling since gravity is not needed up there.

misconceptions.root_belief: things fall only if they are low
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' ideas about orbital motion and gravity

misconceptions.statement: Satellites need engines running all the time to keep going round the Earth.
misconceptions.why: On Earth moving things need continuous push to keep moving.
misconceptions.fix: In space there is almost no air to slow a satellite, so once it has orbital speed it keeps moving without engines. Small thrusters are used only for corrections.

probe.question: After the rocket finishes burning, why does the satellite keep orbiting?
probe.wrong_answer: Its engine keeps pushing it forward all the time.

misconceptions.root_belief: motion needs a continuous force
misconceptions.source_hint: force and motion misconception research (motion implies force)

misconceptions.statement: The Moon is not a satellite because satellites are only man-made machines.
misconceptions.why: The word satellite is mostly heard in the context of ISRO and TV.
misconceptions.fix: A satellite is any object that orbits a planet. The Moon is Earth's natural satellite and Aryabhata, INSAT and others are artificial satellites.

probe.question: Name one natural satellite of Earth.
probe.wrong_answer: There is none; all satellites are made by humans.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: A geostationary satellite is only a few hundred km above Earth like the space station.
misconceptions.why: Students picture all satellites at the same height.
misconceptions.fix: A geostationary satellite is about 36,000 km above the equator, much higher than low-earth satellites at a few hundred km.

probe.question: Roughly how high is a geostationary satellite?
probe.wrong_answer: About 400 km.

misconceptions.root_belief: all things of one kind are the same size

misconceptions.statement: A geostationary satellite is not moving at all.
misconceptions.why: The word stationary means standing still, and it appears fixed in the sky.
misconceptions.fix: It moves at about 3 km every second around Earth, completing one round in 24 hours, the same as Earth's spin, so it seems fixed above one place.

probe.question: Is a geostationary satellite moving? Explain.
probe.wrong_answer: No, it stands still in space above one spot.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: research on frames of reference and relative motion misconceptions

misconceptions.statement: A geostationary satellite stays above one place because Earth's gravity holds it fixed there.
misconceptions.why: Students link staying in place with a strong pull rather than matching speed.
misconceptions.fix: It stays above one place because it goes round in exactly 24 hours, the same time Earth takes to turn once. Gravity only keeps it in orbit.

probe.question: Why does a geostationary satellite stay over the same place?
probe.wrong_answer: Gravity holds it fixed above that spot.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: A geostationary satellite can be placed above any city, such as above the North Pole.
misconceptions.why: Students think orbits can be chosen freely like pins on a globe.
misconceptions.fix: A geostationary orbit must lie directly above the equator. Only there can the satellite's orbit match Earth's spin and stay over one point.

probe.question: Where must a geostationary satellite orbit?
probe.wrong_answer: Above any place we want, even above the pole.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule works everywhere the same way

misconceptions.statement: Satellites closer to Earth move slower because they are closer to the ground.
misconceptions.why: Students link low height with slow speed, like a low-flying kite.
misconceptions.fix: Closer satellites feel stronger gravity and move faster. A LEO satellite goes round in about 90 minutes while a geostationary one takes 24 hours.

probe.question: Which goes round Earth faster, a satellite at 500 km or at 36,000 km?
probe.wrong_answer: The one at 500 km goes slower.

misconceptions.root_belief: closer or lower means slower

misconceptions.statement: A satellite in low-earth orbit can watch one fixed place all day.
misconceptions.why: Students assume any satellite hovers like a geostationary one.
misconceptions.fix: A LEO satellite moves quickly and passes over a place only briefly, then comes back after some time. Watching one place continuously needs a geostationary satellite.

probe.question: Can a polar LEO satellite give constant video of one city?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it stays above the city all day.

misconceptions.root_belief: all things of one kind behave alike

misconceptions.statement: Signals through a satellite reach instantly with no delay at all.
misconceptions.why: Radio and TV seem instantaneous in daily life.
misconceptions.fix: Signals travel at the speed of light, but going 36,000 km up and back takes about a quarter of a second, a small delay.

probe.question: Is there any delay when a signal goes via a geostationary satellite?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it arrives instantly.

misconceptions.root_belief: fast means instant

misconceptions.statement: Mobile phone calls and TV channels come only from towers on the ground, never from satellites.
misconceptions.why: Students see towers everywhere and never see satellites.
misconceptions.fix: Many TV channels and some phone and internet links reach us via communication satellites such as INSAT and GSAT. Dish antennas point at these satellites.

probe.question: How does a DTH dish get TV channels?
probe.wrong_answer: From a nearby ground tower.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Weather satellites control the weather, so they can stop cyclones or bring rain.
misconceptions.why: News says satellites handle cyclones, so students think they act on weather.
misconceptions.fix: Weather satellites only observe clouds, temperature and winds to help forecasts. They cannot change the weather.

probe.question: What can a weather satellite do about an approaching cyclone?
probe.wrong_answer: It can break the cyclone or divert it.

misconceptions.root_belief: watching something means controlling it

misconceptions.statement: Cyclone tracking works from a satellite photo taken at night only with a normal camera, so it fails in the dark.
misconceptions.why: Students assume satellites take ordinary photographs needing sunlight.
misconceptions.fix: Weather satellites also use infrared sensors that detect heat from clouds, so they track cyclones day and night.

probe.question: Can satellites track a cyclone at night?
probe.wrong_answer: No, there is no light for the camera.

misconceptions.root_belief: seeing needs visible light only

misconceptions.statement: A single GPS satellite is enough to find your exact position.
misconceptions.why: Students think one signal gives a place like one map pin.
misconceptions.fix: A receiver needs signals from at least four satellites to find its position and time accurately.

probe.question: How many satellites are needed for a GPS fix?
probe.wrong_answer: Just one.

misconceptions.root_belief: one source is enough

misconceptions.statement: The GPS satellite tracks my phone and sends my location back to it.
misconceptions.why: Phone apps show location, so students think the satellite knows them.
misconceptions.fix: Satellites only broadcast signals with time and position. Your phone's receiver works out its own location from them.

probe.question: Does a GPS satellite know where your phone is?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it tracks it and tells the phone.

misconceptions.root_belief: the sender must know the receiver

misconceptions.statement: NavIC is the same as GPS and is run by America.
misconceptions.why: GPS is the only navigation system most students have heard of.
misconceptions.fix: NavIC is India's own regional navigation system developed by ISRO. GPS is a separate system run by the USA.

probe.question: Which country built NavIC?
probe.wrong_answer: The USA, it is another name for GPS.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding things are the same thing

misconceptions.statement: Satellite images of fields only show pictures; they cannot tell crop health or flood areas.
misconceptions.why: Students think a photo shows only what a normal camera shows.
misconceptions.fix: Sensors record different colours and infrared that show crop health, water, and flood or fire spread. These help in farming and disaster relief.

probe.question: How can satellites help a farmer?
probe.wrong_answer: They cannot, they only take pictures of the land.

misconceptions.root_belief: seeing needs visible light only

misconceptions.statement: PSLV and GSLV are satellites, not rockets.
misconceptions.why: The names are mentioned along with satellites in news.
misconceptions.fix: PSLV and GSLV are launch vehicles (rockets) that carry satellites to orbit. PSLV mainly serves low polar orbits and GSLV serves geostationary orbits.

probe.question: What is PSLV?
probe.wrong_answer: An Indian weather satellite.

misconceptions.root_belief: things named together are the same thing

misconceptions.statement: Rockets move up by pushing against the air, so they cannot work in space.
misconceptions.why: Students see wings and propellers push on air.
misconceptions.fix: A rocket pushes hot gases backwards and the gases push the rocket forward. It does not need air and works best in space.

probe.question: Can a rocket engine work in empty space?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it needs air to push against.

misconceptions.root_belief: pushing needs something to push against
misconceptions.source_hint: research on misconceptions about Newton's third law and rocket propulsion

misconceptions.statement: The whole rocket reaches orbit and the satellite is carried inside it for the whole journey.
misconceptions.why: Pictures show the rocket as a single body going up.
misconceptions.fix: Rocket stages burn out and fall away to lose weight. Only the final stage releases the satellite in orbit.

probe.question: What happens to the lower stages of a rocket?
probe.wrong_answer: They stay attached and reach orbit with the satellite.

misconceptions.root_belief: objects stay in one piece

misconceptions.statement: Satellites in orbit have flat sunlight-free spots so they are always moving in the dark.
misconceptions.why: Space is shown as black.
misconceptions.fix: Satellites in orbit are lit by the Sun on the side facing it and use solar panels for power, with batteries for the time in Earth's shadow.

probe.question: How do most satellites get electric power?
probe.wrong_answer: From fuel burning inside them all the time.

misconceptions.root_belief: space is dark so no sunlight
